newsitem.title: USA: SF Fed's Parry surprised, unfazed by labor data.
newsitem.headline: SF Fed's Parry surprised, unfazed by labor data.

text.p: The U.S. July employment report was somewhat surprising, but still not enough to change the underlying trend of the current economic scenario in the country, said the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

"Those (unemployment) numbers were a bit of a surprise and (it was) quite impressive that the unemployment rate dropped," Robert Parry, the president of the San Francisco Fed told a panel of economists here on Friday.

Parry warned, however, that monthly economic data can be volatile, adding that his perception of the underlying trend for the U.S. economy were not fazed by the labor market numbers reported earlier on Friday.
"I would caution...that on a monthly basis the data are quite volatile," Parry said.
"In my opinion, growth is likely to be relatively moderate, around 2.0 percent or so, over the next several quarters, with inflation being relatively well behaved," he said.

The Labor Department released its employment report for July on Friday, which showed non-farm payrolls grew by 316,000 new jobs, while the unemployment rate dropped to 4.8 percent from 5.0 percent in June.

The report triggered a massive sell-off in the U.S. Treasury market, bringing the benchmark 30-year bond down two full points in active trading on Friday. The bond yield surged to 6.46 percent at the market close on Friday compared with Thursday's closing yield of 6.30 percent.

During a question and answer session after a speech to the Chinese Economists Society, Parry also said a strong dollar and higher productivity, among other things, has helped to keep U.S. inflation low.
"It's quite possible we are seeing an increase in productivity that is enabling companies to increase output without increasing prices," Parry said.
Turning to the dollar the San Francisco Fed chief said a strong U.S. currency has had a positive impact in keeping prices of imports relatively low.
Parry said the pursuit of price stability was desirable in the United States as well as in most industrialized nations.
